01 / THE ASSESSMENT

Capability is growing.
Autonomy needs more evidence.

Strong execution on trained tasks does not establish transfer to unseen tasks, recovery after failure, or unattended operation. This atlas separates reported findings from interpretation.

01GENERALIZATION

A high score has a boundary.

OpenWAM reports 99.3% on LIBERO and 69.2% on LIBERO-Plus, including 33.8% under camera perturbations. These protocols test different conditions.

Our reading Familiar-task success needs a separate robustness test.

OpenWAM v1 · Tables 5 & 13 ↗
02UNSEEN TASKS

Inspect the denominator.

Vid2WAM reports 78.3% across the full suites in its main novel-task setting, but 2.3% on the withheld tasks. Target-task synthetic adaptation is part of this setup.

Our reading A mixed average can obscure unseen-task performance.

Vid2WAM v1 · Tables S11–S12 ↗
03RECOVERY

Six policies. Zero recoveries.

All six policies evaluated in LIBERO-RECOVER score 0% on the LIBERO-100 L4 subset, where obstructing environmental state must be restored.

Scope matters This cohort excludes π0.7, OpenWAM, DreamZero and FLUX 3 Action. It is not an all-current-models claim.

LIBERO-RECOVER v2 · Table 1 ↗
04MEMORY

History can change the result.

SmoLSTM reports 77.5% on LIBERO-Mem, falling to 7.0% when recurrent state is reset every control step. It evaluates held-out initial states after joint training.

Our reading Useful memory is demonstrated; arbitrary unseen memory tasks remain a different claim.

SmoLSTM v1 · Abstract ↗
05WORLD MODELS

Learning from video ≠ generating it at runtime.

Fast-WAM achieves 91.8% on RoboTwin without runtime future generation, versus 90.6% for its joint-generation variant and 83.8% without video co-training.

Our reading Training benefits do not establish a universal need for runtime imagination.

Fast-WAM v2 · Table 1 ↗
06PHYSICAL EVALUATION

Real robots. Small samples.

BFL reports 28/30 completions for FLUX 3 Action and 27/30 for Cosmos 3 Nano in a blinded-operator evaluation run by Positronic Robotics.

Our reading Ten tasks with three attempts each cannot establish a stable general ranking from a one-completion gap.

FLUX 3 Action · Table 6 ↗
PROGRESS IS REAL

π0.7 evaluates instruction following across four unseen kitchens and two unseen bedrooms: 14 scenarios with three to six instructions each. This is concrete environment-transfer evidence, with instruction success as its metric.

π0.7 v2 · §IX-B ↗

02 / READ THE TEST, NOT JUST THE SCORE

There is more than one kind of hard.

These are separate evaluation axes. They are not a difficulty ladder, and benchmark editions can span several axes.

A

Familiar skills

Can the policy execute tasks after task-specific training?

LIBERO · RoboTwin variants
B

Changed conditions

Does it tolerate a new camera, background, object or instruction?

LIBERO-Plus · RoboTwin2.0-Plus
C

New combinations

Can learned skills transfer across a documented task holdout?

RoboCasa365 · RoboDojo Open
D

Necessary memory

Can it act on information no longer visible in the current observation?

CAMP suites · LIBERO-Mem · RMBench
E

Failure recovery

Can it restore the state of the task and continue after an error?

LIBERO-RECOVER
F

Sustained operation

How many jobs finish when retries, resets and interventions count?

Physical long-horizon protocols

05 / FROM BENCHMARK TO DEPLOYMENT

Measure the whole job.

Our proposed industry-facing criteria go beyond an episode success rate. A deployment decision needs the task distribution, intervention process and operating budget.

ANALYST RECOMMENDATION
  1. Completed jobs per hourInclude inference, retries, resets and operator time.
  2. Autonomous completionsState how interventions are defined and counted.
  3. First-attempt and eventual successDisclose time limits and allowed retries.
  4. Recovery and failure recognitionCount false success declarations and failed recovery.
  5. Variation and costTest across environments, days and hardware; report control timing.

06 / HOW TO USE THIS ATLAS

An evidence map, with its limits visible.

Scope & provenance

The assessment focuses on robot manipulation, especially vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action-model (WAM) systems. The catalog also covers adjacent areas. Navigation, locomotion and autonomous driving need their own field assessments.

The research snapshot is dated September 28, 2026. It is a selected literature inventory, not an exhaustive census or live leaderboard. No experiments were rerun.

Numerical findings are author-reported. “Our reading” identifies interpretation, rather than an additional experimental result.

Reading depth is not a quality score.

Paper notes: 44 complete, 59 legacy-unreviewed and four partial. “Complete” describes the note’s recorded reading coverage; it does not mean independent replication.

Catalog resources: targeted protocol review or definition-level discovery. Neither implies a complete paper and code audit.

Popularity: Semantic Scholar citation counts and GitHub repository stars, with retrieval dates. Release milestones usually mean the selected paper’s first arXiv submission; exceptions and date precision are retained.

Source checks behind the assessment

Targeted primary-source checks on September 28, 2026: Vid2WAM v1 (withheld-task appendix tables); π0.7 v2 (evaluation overview and §IX-B); LIBERO-RECOVER v2 (definitions, setup and Table 1); SmoLSTM v1 (abstract only); Fast-WAM v2 (controlled comparisons); FLUX 3 Action (physical-evaluation protocol and Table 6).

OpenWAM v1 reuses the existing complete source audit. Fresh HTML retrieval failed during the assessment. CAMP definitions reuse the earlier catalog review. None of these checks upgraded a paper note’s reading status.

The six-policy recovery cohort comprises π0, π0-FAST, GR00T N1.5, OpenVLA-OFT, Wan2-Policy and Cosmos-Predict2-Policy. Their shared failure is limited to the specified subset and time budget.

The question is not only whether a robot can succeed.
It is how far that success generalizes—and what happens when it does not.
